content_json.title: Present Simple, Present Continuous, Present Perfect, and Present Perfect Continuous – Inverse Thinking for Vietnamese Learners

components.text: Listen & Spot Errors

Play a 60‑second audio clip of Vietnamese learners making typical present‑tense mistakes (e.g., 'I am knowing him for two years', 'She go to school every day'). Listen carefully and note which verb forms sound wrong.

components.body: Focus on the time markers (for, since, every day) and whether the verb describes a state or an action.

components.text: Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
1. Identify common Vietnamese‑speaker errors in the four present tenses.
2. Explain why each erroneous sentence violates grammar rules, referencing time markers and verb form constraints.
3. Correct erroneous sentences into the appropriate present tense form.
4. Analyze a short mixed‑tense paragraph and justify tense choices for each verb.
5. Create an original mini‑dialogue that correctly deploys all four present tenses in meaningful context.
Common Mistakes & Why They're Wrong

steps.title: Identify the error
steps.body: Look at the sentence and spot the verb form that does not match the time marker or verb type.

steps.title: Name the rule
steps.body: Recall the rule for the present simple, continuous, perfect, or perfect continuous that applies.

steps.title: Produce the correction
steps.body: Rewrite the sentence using the correct verb form and, if needed, adjust the time marker.

components.title: Remember
components.body: Stative verbs (know, believe, belong, etc.) are not used in continuous forms.

rows: I am knowing him for two years.
I have known him for two years.
Know is a stative verb; use present perfect with for/since.
She go to school every day.
She goes to school every day.
Third‑person singular needs -s in present simple.
I have lived here since 5 years.
I have lived here for five years.
Since points to a specific start; for is used with a length of time.
We are having breakfast at 8 a.m. every morning.
We have breakfast at 8 a.m. every morning.
Habitual actions use present simple, not continuous.
They have been waiting for the bus since 20 minutes.
They have been waiting for the bus for 20 minutes.
For + length of time with present perfect continuous.

Create Your Own Dialogue

In pairs, write a 10‑line mini‑dialogue about a Vietnamese student's daily routine. The dialogue must correctly use at least one example of each present tense: present simple, present continuous, present perfect, and present perfect continuous.

Answer Key

questions.text: I ______ (know) him since we were children.
questions.explain: Since indicates a starting point in the past continuing to now → present perfect.

questions.text: She ______ (go) to the gym three times a week.
We ______ (live) in Hanoi for ten years.
questions.explain: For + length of time with a result up to now → present perfect.
Action happening at the moment of speaking → present continuous.

questions.text: They ______ (wait) for the bus for over an hour.
questions.explain: For + length of time with ongoing action → present perfect continuous.
Completed action with unspecified time → present perfect.
Stative verb understand → present simple negative.

content_json.title: Present Tenses – Inverse Thinking Worksheet for Vietnamese Learners

components.text: This worksheet uses inverse thinking: instead of starting with rules, you start with errors that Vietnamese learners often make. For each item, first identify the mistake, then explain the rule it breaks, and finally write the correct sentence. Read every sentence carefully and pay attention to time markers (every day, since, for, right now, etc.) and verb types (action vs. stative).
Quick Reference: Form and Typical Use of the Four Present Tenses

rows: Habits, routines, facts (every day, always, usually)
Actions happening now or around now (now, right now, at the moment)
Past action with present relevance; unfinished time (just, already, yet, since + point, for + duration)
Action started in the past, still continuing; emphasizes duration (for, since, all morning)
components.caption: Use this table as a reference while you complete Parts A–D.

components.title: Three Common Vietnamese-Learner Errors
components.body:
1. Using stative verbs (know, like, want, need, belong, love) in continuous form — e.g., 'I am knowing him' is wrong.
2. Forgetting the third-person singular -s/-es in Present Simple — e.g., 'She go to school' should be 'She goes to school.'
3. Mixing up Present Perfect and Present Perfect Continuous, or using 'since' with a duration and 'for' with a point in time.

components.text: Read each sentence carefully. Choose A, B, C, or D that correctly identifies the type of error in the underlined part. Circle your choice.

Error in: "I am knowing him for two years."
What rule is being broken?

Error in: "She go to school every day."
What rule is being broken?

Error in: "I have been lived in Hanoi since 2020."
What rule is being broken?

Rewrite each sentence so that it is grammatically correct. Then, in one short sentence, name the rule you applied (e.g., 'Since + point in time → for + duration' or 'Habitual action → Present Simple').

Correct this sentence and explain the rule:
'I have lived here since five years.'

Correct this sentence and explain the rule:
'They are watching TV every evening.'

Correct this sentence and explain the rule:
'He has been went to Hanoi last week.'

Correct this sentence and explain the rule:
'My brother don't like coffee, but he is wanting some tea.'
Read the paragraph about Mai's daily routine. For each underlined verb phrase, write the tense name in column 3 and a brief justification in column 4 (cite the time marker, the verb type, or both).

Paragraph: 'Every morning, Mai (1) gets up at 6 a.m. Right now, she (2) is studying for her English test. She (3) has lived in Hanoi for five years. She (4) has been studying English since 2020. After class, she usually (5) walks home with her friends.'

Work with a partner. Together, write a 10-line dialogue about a Vietnamese student's daily routine. Your dialogue must correctly use all four present tenses at least once. Label each line with the speaker (A or B).

components.title: Distribution Suggestion
components.body: Lines 1–2: Present Simple (habits). Lines 3–4: Present Continuous (now / at the moment). Lines 5–6: Present Perfect (with for/since/already/just). Lines 7–8: Present Perfect Continuous (with for/since, focus on duration). Lines 9–10: any mix, but each line must be grammatically correct.

components.instruction: Read your completed dialogue aloud with your partner. After you finish, swap roles and present it to the class.

components.text: Part A – Error Identification

rows: Stative verb 'know' expresses a state, not a dynamic action, so it cannot be used in continuous form. Correct: 'I have known him for two years.'
Third-person singular subject 'She' requires -s/-es in Present Simple. Correct: 'She goes to school every day.'
Present Perfect Continuous = have/has + been + V-ing. 'been lived' uses the past participle instead of the -ing form. Correct: 'I have been living in Hanoi since 2020.'

components.text: Part B – Error Correction

rows: I have lived here for five years.
'Since' is used with a point in time (since 2020, since Monday). 'For' is used with a duration (for five years).
Habitual actions with time markers like 'every evening', 'always', 'usually' take Present Simple, not Present Continuous.
He went to Hanoi last week.
'Last week' refers to a finished past time → Past Simple, not Perfect Continuous. Present Perfect Continuous cannot be used with finished-time markers.
My brother doesn't like coffee, but he wants some tea.
Two errors: (1) Present Simple needs 'doesn't' with third-person singular; (2) 'want' is a stative verb and cannot take the continuous form.

components.text: Part C – Paragraph Analysis

rows: 'Right now' = action happening at the moment of speaking.
'for five years' + result/state that continues up to now; the speaker emphasizes the present situation, not the duration of the activity.
'since 2020' = action that began in the past and is still continuing; emphasizes duration of the activity.

components.text: Part D – Sample Mini-Dialogue (Model Answer)

components.instruction: This is a model answer. Accept any student dialogue that (a) uses all four present tenses, (b) has no grammatical errors in verb form, and (c) uses appropriate time markers.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: I usually get up at six o'clock every morning.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Really? I always have breakfast with my family before school.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Look at me — I am studying English right now.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I am waiting for the school bus at the moment.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: I have lived in Ho Chi Minh City for ten years.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I have just finished my homework.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: I have been practicing the piano since I was seven.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: She has been learning English for six months already.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: We often meet after class to review the lesson.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Today we are preparing for the speaking test together.

content_json.title: Present Tenses Mastery Quiz – Inverse Thinking for Vietnamese Learners

components.text: Four Tenses, Three Frequent Pitfalls

This quiz tests your ability to spot and correct the three most common errors Vietnamese learners make with present tenses: (1) using stative verbs like know, want, love in any continuous form, (2) forgetting the third-person singular -s in present simple, and (3) confusing present perfect simple with present perfect continuous, especially with since/for and result vs. duration.

components.title: Quick reference
components.body: Present Simple = routine or permanent truth. Present Continuous = action happening now or a temporary situation around now. Present Perfect Simple = past action with a present result. Present Perfect Continuous = past action continuing to now, emphasis on duration.

rows: now, right now, at the moment, currently, Look!
since, for, already, yet, just, ever, never, so far
She has worked here for 5 years.
since, for, recently, lately, all morning
She has been working here since 2020.

sections.title: Part A – Choose the Grammatically Correct Sentence

components.text: Which sentence correctly expresses 'I have known him for two years'?

options.A: I am knowing him for two years.
options.B: I have known him for two years.
options.C: I have been knowing him for two years.
options.D: I am knowing him since two years.

components.explain: Know is a stative verb — it describes a state, not a dynamic action, so it cannot appear in any continuous form (-ing). The present perfect simple (have known) with 'for' is the correct form to express a state that started in the past and continues to the present.

wrong_reasons.A: 'Know' is stative; it cannot be used in the present continuous.
wrong_reasons.C: The present perfect continuous is also ungrammatical with stative verbs; only the simple form is allowed.
wrong_reasons.D: Two errors combine: 'know' is stative (no -ing), and 'since' must be followed by a point in time, not a duration like 'two years'.

components.essence: Stative verbs (know, love, want, believe, own, need) reject all continuous forms.
components.tip: If the verb describes a state rather than an action, never add -ing.

components.text: She ___ to school every day.
components.explain: With a third-person singular subject (She/He/It) and a habitual action marked by 'every day', the present simple requires the -s/-es ending on the verb.

wrong_reasons.A: Missing the third-person singular -s; the base form 'go' is used with I/you/we/they.
wrong_reasons.C: Present continuous suggests a temporary action happening now, not a daily routine.
wrong_reasons.D: Present perfect implies a connection to the present moment, which conflicts with the routine meaning of 'every day'.

components.essence: Third-person singular subjects require -s/-es in present simple affirmative.
components.tip: He/She/It → add -s. After -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o, add -es (go → goes, watch → watches, do → does).

components.text: Look! The children ___ in the garden right now.
components.explain: The time markers 'Look!' and 'right now' signal an action happening at the moment of speaking, which requires the present continuous (are playing).

wrong_reasons.A: Present simple expresses routines or general truths, not actions happening right now.
wrong_reasons.B: Third-person -s with present simple does not match the 'right now' context.
wrong_reasons.D: Present perfect is not used for actions visibly in progress at this very moment.

components.essence: Actions happening now require present continuous.
components.tip: Trigger words: now, right now, at the moment, currently, Look!, Listen!

components.text: I ___ English for five years, and I still study it every week.
components.explain: The action started in the past and is still continuing, with emphasis on the duration ('for five years'). Present perfect continuous (have been learning) emphasizes how long the activity has been ongoing up to now, and pairs naturally with 'still' in the second clause.

wrong_reasons.A: Present simple implies a permanent state but does not capture the five-year duration from past to present.
wrong_reasons.B: Present continuous describes only the current moment, not a five-year duration.
wrong_reasons.C: Present perfect simple is grammatically possible but emphasizes the result (I know English) rather than the ongoing duration; the follow-up 'still study it every week' shows the activity is still in progress, favoring the continuous form.

components.essence: Duration emphasized + activity still continuing + dynamic verb → present perfect continuous.
components.tip: How long + still continuing? → 'have been V-ing'. How much / how many results? → 'have V3'.

sections.title: Part B – Spot and Correct Vietnamese-Learner Errors

components.text: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

options.B: I am living here for 5 years.
options.C: I have lived here since 5 years.
options.D: I have been living here for 5 years.

components.explain: 'Since' must be followed by a point in time (since 2019, since Monday), not a duration. 'For' is used with durations (for 5 years, for a long time). Present perfect continuous (have been living) is preferred for a continuing action emphasizing duration.

wrong_reasons.A: Present simple cannot pair with 'since + duration', and 'since' requires a point in time.
wrong_reasons.B: Present continuous describes only the current moment and cannot pair with 'for 5 years'.
wrong_reasons.C: Two errors: 'since' is wrong before a duration (should be 'for' or replace '5 years' with a year), and the tense is not the best fit for emphasizing ongoing duration.

components.essence: since + point in time (2019, Monday, I was a child); for + duration (5 years, a long time, 3 months).
components.tip: If you see a number of years with 'since', change 'since' to 'for' or the years to a starting year.

components.text: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

options.A: He is wanting a new phone.
options.C: He has been wanting a new phone since months.
options.D: He is wanting a new phone for months.

components.explain: 'Want' is a stative verb expressing a mental state. It cannot appear in any continuous form (-ing). The correct form is present simple (wants).

wrong_reasons.A: 'Want' is stative; present continuous is ungrammatical here.
wrong_reasons.C: 'Want' is stative, so 'has been wanting' is ungrammatical; also 'since' must be followed by a point in time, not 'months'.
wrong_reasons.D: Two errors: 'want' is stative (no -ing), and present continuous cannot pair with 'for months'.

components.essence: Stative verbs reject all progressive / continuous forms.
components.tip: Common stative verbs to memorize: know, want, like, love, hate, believe, own, need, understand, prefer, seem, belong.

components.text: My sister ___ English since she was ten years old.
components.explain: 'Since she was ten years old' marks a starting point in the past, and the action continues to the present. Present perfect continuous (has been studying) emphasizes this ongoing duration, which is the preferred form with dynamic verbs like 'study' in this context.

wrong_reasons.A: Present simple cannot pair with 'since + past point' to describe an action continuing to now.
wrong_reasons.B: Present continuous describes only the moment of speaking, not a duration from age ten.
wrong_reasons.C: Present perfect simple is grammatically possible, but it emphasizes the result (she knows English) rather than the ongoing duration; the 'since' phrase with a dynamic verb strongly favors the continuous form.

components.essence: since + point in time + continuing action + dynamic verb → present perfect continuous.
components.tip: Dynamic verbs (study, work, live, learn, wait) + 'since' → 'have been V-ing' for emphasis on duration.

components.text: Which sentence uses the correct tense for a temporary action happening around now?

options.A: She works part-time at a café this month.
options.B: She is working part-time at a café this month.
options.C: She has worked part-time at a café this month.
options.D: She has been working part-time at a café this month.

components.explain: 'This month' signals a temporary, time-bounded situation around the present. Present continuous (is working) is the natural choice for a temporary action in progress around now, contrasting with a permanent or long-term job.

wrong_reasons.A: Present simple implies a routine or permanent job, which contradicts the temporary 'this month' frame.
wrong_reasons.C: Present perfect simple emphasizes the result or completion, not the temporary ongoing nature.
wrong_reasons.D: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration from a past point; while not strictly wrong, it is less natural than present continuous for a clearly time-bounded temporary action marked by 'this month'.

components.essence: Temporary situations around now → present continuous.
components.tip: this week / this month / this term / nowadays / these days → present continuous for temporary situations.

components.text: Read the paragraph, then choose the correct verb form for blanks (1) and (4). 'Lan (1) ___ a student at Hanoi High School. She gets up at six every morning. Right now, she is reviewing for her English test. She (4) ___ English for seven years, but she is studying harder lately because the exam is next week.'
Which verb form correctly fills blank (1)?
components.explain: The blank describes Lan's current identity and role. 'Is' (present simple) expresses a current state that holds during her school years. 'Has been a student' would suggest a temporary status that may change soon, which is not the intended meaning.

wrong_reasons.B: Present perfect continuous is incorrect because 'be' is stative; it also implies a temporary status, not a permanent school identity.
wrong_reasons.C: 'Has' alone is ungrammatical without a past participle; it would need to be 'has been'.

components.essence: Identity roles and long-term states → present simple 'is / am / are'.
components.tip: He/She/It + is for current states and roles; use 'has been' only when the state is clearly temporary.

components.text: Which verb form correctly fills blank (4)?
components.explain: 'For seven years' marks a duration from a past starting point to the present. Present perfect continuous (has been studying) emphasizes the ongoing duration of study. The follow-up clause 'but she is studying harder lately' reinforces that the activity is still continuing and intensifying.

wrong_reasons.A: Present simple cannot pair with 'for seven years' to describe an action continuing to now.
wrong_reasons.B: Present continuous describes only the current moment, not a seven-year duration.
wrong_reasons.C: Present perfect simple is grammatically possible, but it emphasizes the result rather than the ongoing effort; the 'lately' clue in the next sentence favors the continuous form.

components.essence: Long duration + still continuing + 'lately' signal → present perfect continuous.
components.tip: If the next sentence mentions a recent change or intensification ('lately', 'recently', 'these days'), prefer the perfect continuous form.

components.text: Full Answer Key

rows: Using 'am knowing' or 'have been knowing' (stative misuse)
Forgetting third-person -s ('She go' instead of 'She goes')
Using present simple for actions happening now
Using present perfect simple when duration is emphasized
Using continuous with stative verbs ('is wanting')
Using present simple or present perfect simple with 'since'
Choosing perfect simple over perfect continuous for duration

components.title: Scoring Guide
components.body: Each question is worth 1 point. 9–10 correct: Excellent — ready to produce original sentences using all four tenses. 7–8 correct: Good — review the wrong answers and study the related tense row in the overview table. 5–6 correct: Fair — revisit form, time markers, and since/for rules before retaking. Below 5: Re-study the four-tense chart in the overview and redo the quiz.

components.title: Discussion Prompts for After the Quiz
components.body: 1. Why can't we say 'I am knowing him' or 'I have been knowing him'? 2. When is 'since' wrong with a number of years? 3. How do you decide between present perfect simple and present perfect continuous? 4. Which Vietnamese sentence structure tempts you to forget the -s ending?

components.title: Re-teach Trigger
components.body: If more than 40% of the class misses the same question (especially q1, q2, q5, or q6), pause and re-teach that tense cluster before moving to the production task in the next lesson phase.

Answer Key

questions.text: I ______ (know) him since we were children.
questions.explain: Since indicates a starting point in the past continuing to now → present perfect.

questions.text: She ______ (go) to the gym three times a week.
We ______ (live) in Hanoi for ten years.
questions.explain: For + length of time with a result up to now → present perfect.
Action happening at the moment of speaking → present continuous.

questions.text: They ______ (wait) for the bus for over an hour.
questions.explain: For + length of time with ongoing action → present perfect continuous.
Completed action with unspecified time → present perfect.
Stative verb understand → present simple negative.

artifacts.title: Present Tenses – Inverse Thinking Worksheet for Vietnamese Learners

components.text: This worksheet uses inverse thinking: instead of starting with rules, you start with errors that Vietnamese learners often make. For each item, first identify the mistake, then explain the rule it breaks, and finally write the correct sentence. Read every sentence carefully and pay attention to time markers (every day, since, for, right now, etc.) and verb types (action vs. stative).
Quick Reference: Form and Typical Use of the Four Present Tenses

rows: Habits, routines, facts (every day, always, usually)
Actions happening now or around now (now, right now, at the moment)
Past action with present relevance; unfinished time (just, already, yet, since + point, for + duration)
Action started in the past, still continuing; emphasizes duration (for, since, all morning)
components.caption: Use this table as a reference while you complete Parts A–D.

components.title: Three Common Vietnamese-Learner Errors
components.body:
1. Using stative verbs (know, like, want, need, belong, love) in continuous form — e.g., 'I am knowing him' is wrong.
2. Forgetting the third-person singular -s/-es in Present Simple — e.g., 'She go to school' should be 'She goes to school.'
3. Mixing up Present Perfect and Present Perfect Continuous, or using 'since' with a duration and 'for' with a point in time.

components.text: Read each sentence carefully. Choose A, B, C, or D that correctly identifies the type of error in the underlined part. Circle your choice.

Error in: "I am knowing him for two years."
What rule is being broken?

Error in: "She go to school every day."
What rule is being broken?

Error in: "I have been lived in Hanoi since 2020."
What rule is being broken?

Rewrite each sentence so that it is grammatically correct. Then, in one short sentence, name the rule you applied (e.g., 'Since + point in time → for + duration' or 'Habitual action → Present Simple').

Correct this sentence and explain the rule:
'I have lived here since five years.'

Correct this sentence and explain the rule:
'They are watching TV every evening.'

Correct this sentence and explain the rule:
'He has been went to Hanoi last week.'

Correct this sentence and explain the rule:
'My brother don't like coffee, but he is wanting some tea.'
Read the paragraph about Mai's daily routine. For each underlined verb phrase, write the tense name in column 3 and a brief justification in column 4 (cite the time marker, the verb type, or both).

Paragraph: 'Every morning, Mai (1) gets up at 6 a.m. Right now, she (2) is studying for her English test. She (3) has lived in Hanoi for five years. She (4) has been studying English since 2020. After class, she usually (5) walks home with her friends.'

Work with a partner. Together, write a 10-line dialogue about a Vietnamese student's daily routine. Your dialogue must correctly use all four present tenses at least once. Label each line with the speaker (A or B).

components.title: Distribution Suggestion
components.body: Lines 1–2: Present Simple (habits). Lines 3–4: Present Continuous (now / at the moment). Lines 5–6: Present Perfect (with for/since/already/just). Lines 7–8: Present Perfect Continuous (with for/since, focus on duration). Lines 9–10: any mix, but each line must be grammatically correct.

components.instruction: Read your completed dialogue aloud with your partner. After you finish, swap roles and present it to the class.

components.text: Part A – Error Identification

rows: Stative verb 'know' expresses a state, not a dynamic action, so it cannot be used in continuous form. Correct: 'I have known him for two years.'
Third-person singular subject 'She' requires -s/-es in Present Simple. Correct: 'She goes to school every day.'
Present Perfect Continuous = have/has + been + V-ing. 'been lived' uses the past participle instead of the -ing form. Correct: 'I have been living in Hanoi since 2020.'

components.text: Part B – Error Correction

rows: I have lived here for five years.
'Since' is used with a point in time (since 2020, since Monday). 'For' is used with a duration (for five years).
Habitual actions with time markers like 'every evening', 'always', 'usually' take Present Simple, not Present Continuous.
He went to Hanoi last week.
'Last week' refers to a finished past time → Past Simple, not Perfect Continuous. Present Perfect Continuous cannot be used with finished-time markers.
My brother doesn't like coffee, but he wants some tea.
Two errors: (1) Present Simple needs 'doesn't' with third-person singular; (2) 'want' is a stative verb and cannot take the continuous form.

components.text: Part C – Paragraph Analysis

rows: 'Right now' = action happening at the moment of speaking.
'for five years' + result/state that continues up to now; the speaker emphasizes the present situation, not the duration of the activity.
'since 2020' = action that began in the past and is still continuing; emphasizes duration of the activity.

metadata.topic: Present Simple, Present Continuous, Present Perfect, Present Perfect Continuous

artifacts.title: Present Tenses Mastery Quiz – Inverse Thinking for Vietnamese Learners

components.text: Four Tenses, Three Frequent Pitfalls

This quiz tests your ability to spot and correct the three most common errors Vietnamese learners make with present tenses: (1) using stative verbs like know, want, love in any continuous form, (2) forgetting the third-person singular -s in present simple, and (3) confusing present perfect simple with present perfect continuous, especially with since/for and result vs. duration.

components.title: Quick reference
components.body: Present Simple = routine or permanent truth. Present Continuous = action happening now or a temporary situation around now. Present Perfect Simple = past action with a present result. Present Perfect Continuous = past action continuing to now, emphasis on duration.

rows: now, right now, at the moment, currently, Look!
since, for, already, yet, just, ever, never, so far
She has worked here for 5 years.
since, for, recently, lately, all morning
She has been working here since 2020.

sections.title: Part A – Choose the Grammatically Correct Sentence

components.text: Which sentence correctly expresses 'I have known him for two years'?

options.A: I am knowing him for two years.
options.B: I have known him for two years.
options.C: I have been knowing him for two years.
options.D: I am knowing him since two years.

components.explain: Know is a stative verb — it describes a state, not a dynamic action, so it cannot appear in any continuous form (-ing). The present perfect simple (have known) with 'for' is the correct form to express a state that started in the past and continues to the present.

wrong_reasons.A: 'Know' is stative; it cannot be used in the present continuous.
wrong_reasons.C: The present perfect continuous is also ungrammatical with stative verbs; only the simple form is allowed.
wrong_reasons.D: Two errors combine: 'know' is stative (no -ing), and 'since' must be followed by a point in time, not a duration like 'two years'.

components.essence: Stative verbs (know, love, want, believe, own, need) reject all continuous forms.
components.tip: If the verb describes a state rather than an action, never add -ing.

components.text: She ___ to school every day.
components.explain: With a third-person singular subject (She/He/It) and a habitual action marked by 'every day', the present simple requires the -s/-es ending on the verb.

wrong_reasons.A: Missing the third-person singular -s; the base form 'go' is used with I/you/we/they.
wrong_reasons.C: Present continuous suggests a temporary action happening now, not a daily routine.
wrong_reasons.D: Present perfect implies a connection to the present moment, which conflicts with the routine meaning of 'every day'.

components.essence: Third-person singular subjects require -s/-es in present simple affirmative.
components.tip: He/She/It → add -s. After -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o, add -es (go → goes, watch → watches, do → does).

components.text: Look! The children ___ in the garden right now.
components.explain: The time markers 'Look!' and 'right now' signal an action happening at the moment of speaking, which requires the present continuous (are playing).

wrong_reasons.A: Present simple expresses routines or general truths, not actions happening right now.
wrong_reasons.B: Third-person -s with present simple does not match the 'right now' context.
wrong_reasons.D: Present perfect is not used for actions visibly in progress at this very moment.

components.essence: Actions happening now require present continuous.
components.tip: Trigger words: now, right now, at the moment, currently, Look!, Listen!

components.text: I ___ English for five years, and I still study it every week.
components.explain: The action started in the past and is still continuing, with emphasis on the duration ('for five years'). Present perfect continuous (have been learning) emphasizes how long the activity has been ongoing up to now, and pairs naturally with 'still' in the second clause.

wrong_reasons.A: Present simple implies a permanent state but does not capture the five-year duration from past to present.
wrong_reasons.B: Present continuous describes only the current moment, not a five-year duration.
wrong_reasons.C: Present perfect simple is grammatically possible but emphasizes the result (I know English) rather than the ongoing duration; the follow-up 'still study it every week' shows the activity is still in progress, favoring the continuous form.

components.essence: Duration emphasized + activity still continuing + dynamic verb → present perfect continuous.
components.tip: How long + still continuing? → 'have been V-ing'. How much / how many results? → 'have V3'.

sections.title: Part B – Spot and Correct Vietnamese-Learner Errors

components.text: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

options.B: I am living here for 5 years.
options.C: I have lived here since 5 years.
options.D: I have been living here for 5 years.

components.explain: 'Since' must be followed by a point in time (since 2019, since Monday), not a duration. 'For' is used with durations (for 5 years, for a long time). Present perfect continuous (have been living) is preferred for a continuing action emphasizing duration.

wrong_reasons.A: Present simple cannot pair with 'since + duration', and 'since' requires a point in time.
wrong_reasons.B: Present continuous describes only the current moment and cannot pair with 'for 5 years'.
wrong_reasons.C: Two errors: 'since' is wrong before a duration (should be 'for' or replace '5 years' with a year), and the tense is not the best fit for emphasizing ongoing duration.

components.essence: since + point in time (2019, Monday, I was a child); for + duration (5 years, a long time, 3 months).
components.tip: If you see a number of years with 'since', change 'since' to 'for' or the years to a starting year.

components.text: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

options.A: He is wanting a new phone.
options.C: He has been wanting a new phone since months.
options.D: He is wanting a new phone for months.

components.explain: 'Want' is a stative verb expressing a mental state. It cannot appear in any continuous form (-ing). The correct form is present simple (wants).

wrong_reasons.A: 'Want' is stative; present continuous is ungrammatical here.
wrong_reasons.C: 'Want' is stative, so 'has been wanting' is ungrammatical; also 'since' must be followed by a point in time, not 'months'.
wrong_reasons.D: Two errors: 'want' is stative (no -ing), and present continuous cannot pair with 'for months'.

components.essence: Stative verbs reject all progressive / continuous forms.
components.tip: Common stative verbs to memorize: know, want, like, love, hate, believe, own, need, understand, prefer, seem, belong.

components.text: My sister ___ English since she was ten years old.
components.explain: 'Since she was ten years old' marks a starting point in the past, and the action continues to the present. Present perfect continuous (has been studying) emphasizes this ongoing duration, which is the preferred form with dynamic verbs like 'study' in this context.

wrong_reasons.A: Present simple cannot pair with 'since + past point' to describe an action continuing to now.
wrong_reasons.B: Present continuous describes only the moment of speaking, not a duration from age ten.
wrong_reasons.C: Present perfect simple is grammatically possible, but it emphasizes the result (she knows English) rather than the ongoing duration; the 'since' phrase with a dynamic verb strongly favors the continuous form.

components.essence: since + point in time + continuing action + dynamic verb → present perfect continuous.
components.tip: Dynamic verbs (study, work, live, learn, wait) + 'since' → 'have been V-ing' for emphasis on duration.

components.text: Which sentence uses the correct tense for a temporary action happening around now?

options.A: She works part-time at a café this month.
options.B: She is working part-time at a café this month.
options.C: She has worked part-time at a café this month.
options.D: She has been working part-time at a café this month.

components.explain: 'This month' signals a temporary, time-bounded situation around the present. Present continuous (is working) is the natural choice for a temporary action in progress around now, contrasting with a permanent or long-term job.

wrong_reasons.A: Present simple implies a routine or permanent job, which contradicts the temporary 'this month' frame.
wrong_reasons.C: Present perfect simple emphasizes the result or completion, not the temporary ongoing nature.
wrong_reasons.D: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration from a past point; while not strictly wrong, it is less natural than present continuous for a clearly time-bounded temporary action marked by 'this month'.

components.essence: Temporary situations around now → present continuous.
components.tip: this week / this month / this term / nowadays / these days → present continuous for temporary situations.

components.text: Read the paragraph, then choose the correct verb form for blanks (1) and (4). 'Lan (1) ___ a student at Hanoi High School. She gets up at six every morning. Right now, she is reviewing for her English test. She (4) ___ English for seven years, but she is studying harder lately because the exam is next week.'
Which verb form correctly fills blank (1)?
components.explain: The blank describes Lan's current identity and role. 'Is' (present simple) expresses a current state that holds during her school years. 'Has been a student' would suggest a temporary status that may change soon, which is not the intended meaning.

wrong_reasons.B: Present perfect continuous is incorrect because 'be' is stative; it also implies a temporary status, not a permanent school identity.
wrong_reasons.C: 'Has' alone is ungrammatical without a past participle; it would need to be 'has been'.

components.essence: Identity roles and long-term states → present simple 'is / am / are'.
components.tip: He/She/It + is for current states and roles; use 'has been' only when the state is clearly temporary.

components.text: Which verb form correctly fills blank (4)?
components.explain: 'For seven years' marks a duration from a past starting point to the present. Present perfect continuous (has been studying) emphasizes the ongoing duration of study. The follow-up clause 'but she is studying harder lately' reinforces that the activity is still continuing and intensifying.

wrong_reasons.A: Present simple cannot pair with 'for seven years' to describe an action continuing to now.
wrong_reasons.B: Present continuous describes only the current moment, not a seven-year duration.
wrong_reasons.C: Present perfect simple is grammatically possible, but it emphasizes the result rather than the ongoing effort; the 'lately' clue in the next sentence favors the continuous form.

components.essence: Long duration + still continuing + 'lately' signal → present perfect continuous.
components.tip: If the next sentence mentions a recent change or intensification ('lately', 'recently', 'these days'), prefer the perfect continuous form.

components.text: Full Answer Key

rows: Using 'am knowing' or 'have been knowing' (stative misuse)
Forgetting third-person -s ('She go' instead of 'She goes')
Using present simple for actions happening now
Using present perfect simple when duration is emphasized
Using continuous with stative verbs ('is wanting')
Using present simple or present perfect simple with 'since'
Choosing perfect simple over perfect continuous for duration

components.title: Scoring Guide
components.body: Each question is worth 1 point. 9–10 correct: Excellent — ready to produce original sentences using all four tenses. 7–8 correct: Good — review the wrong answers and study the related tense row in the overview table. 5–6 correct: Fair — revisit form, time markers, and since/for rules before retaking. Below 5: Re-study the four-tense chart in the overview and redo the quiz.

components.title: Discussion Prompts for After the Quiz
components.body: 1. Why can't we say 'I am knowing him' or 'I have been knowing him'? 2. When is 'since' wrong with a number of years? 3. How do you decide between present perfect simple and present perfect continuous? 4. Which Vietnamese sentence structure tempts you to forget the -s ending?

components.title: Re-teach Trigger
components.body: If more than 40% of the class misses the same question (especially q1, q2, q5, or q6), pause and re-teach that tense cluster before moving to the production task in the next lesson phase.
